code.title: Rich entity guards its own rule

followUps:
Search for the meaning of the rule, not one spelling of it, and let tests prove you found every copy.

Steps: grep for the constants and status names the rule uses ("SHIPPED", 30 days); find every caller of the setter that changes that field; search for the same condition written differently (status != X, !isShipped()). Then write one characterization test per found place. Finally move the rule into one method, such as order.cancel(), and delete the setter so the compiler lists any copy you missed.

An anemic model is fine when the area really has almost no rules, such as admin settings, reference data or a simple catalogue.

If a screen only saves and loads fields, with no rule beyond "name is required", a plain record plus a repository is quicker to write and easier to read than rich objects. The warning sign to switch is when you copy the same if into a second service. Two copies of a rule mean it should live in the entity. Data transfer objects and read models are also meant to be plain data.

code.title: Constructor injection with a fake in tests
code.python:
class Greeter:
    """The service receives its dependencies; it never builds them itself."""
    def __init__(self, clock, mailer):
        self.clock = clock
        self.mailer = mailer

    def greet(self, name):
        part = "morning" if self.clock() < 12 else "afternoon"
        self.mailer("Good " + part + ", " + name)


# Composition root: build concrete objects and wire them
Greeter(lambda: 9, lambda m: print("real mailer: " + m)).greet("Asha")
# Test: same class, fake dependencies
sent = []
Greeter(lambda: 15, sent.append).greet("Ravi")
print("fake captured: " + sent[0])

followUps:
With dependency injection the class is handed what it needs; with a service locator the class goes and asks a global registry for it.

The locator hides dependencies: the constructor looks empty, so you only discover them at run time as a missing-binding error, and tests must set up the global registry. With injection, new OrderService(repo, pay) shows everything needed in the signature. Prefer injection; a locator is tolerable only at the very edge (the composition root, or a framework hook you cannot change).

A captive dependency is a short-lived object trapped inside a long-lived one, so it lives far longer than it should.

Example: a singleton ReportService takes a per-request DbSession in its constructor. The singleton is built once, so every request now shares request 1's session: stale data, thread-safety bugs, a closed connection. The rule is that an object may only depend on objects with a lifetime equal to or longer than its own. Fix by injecting a factory or provider (Supplier<DbSession>) and asking it per call.

A tiny container is a map of bindings plus one recursive resolve function with a singleton cache.

Map<Class,Supplier<Object>> binds; Map<Class,Object> cache;
Object get(Class t) {
  return cache.computeIfAbsent(t, k -> binds.get(k).get());
}
// a binding calls get() for its own parameters:
bind(OrderService.class, () -> new OrderService(get(Repo.class), get(Pay.class)));

Add a resolution stack for cycle errors and you have the core of Guice. Cost: O(number of types) once, then O(1) lookups.

code.title: DI container: resolution stack and cycle detection

followUps:
Scope decides whether the container reuses a cached object or builds a new one for each request, so it changes only the cache step of resolution.

Singleton: one instance in a global cache. Prototype (transient): never cached, so each of the 3 parameters asking for Clock gets a fresh one. Request: cached in a per-request map that is thrown away when the request ends. The graph walk and cycle check are identical; only the cache that is checked and filled differs. Watch for longer-lived objects holding shorter-lived ones.

Dagger does the same graph walk at compile time and writes plain Java code, instead of using reflection at start-up.

The annotation processor reads @Inject constructors and @Module bindings, checks that every parameter has a binding, rejects cycles, and generates a component class that calls new in the right order. Result: missing bindings and cycles are compile errors, not start-up crashes; there is no reflection cost; and it works well on Android. The trade-off is less runtime flexibility (no adding a binding while running) and longer builds.

You unload a plugin by dropping every reference to it and its class loader, so the garbage collector can free it.

Steps: call stop() so it closes threads, sockets and timers; remove it from the registry; cancel its scheduled tasks; clear any listeners it registered with the host. In Java, each plugin has its own URLClassLoader; once nothing points at the loader, the classes and static data are collected. Leaks come from a leftover thread, a ThreadLocal or a host-side cache that still holds a plugin object. For untrusted or leaky code, run it in a separate process and kill it.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a plugin system where the host is an AI app and each plugin is a separate server process.

The shape matches: a small stable contract (list tools, call tool with JSON arguments), discovery by configuration, version negotiation when connecting, and isolation because each server is its own process, so a crash or hang does not take down the host. The same safety rules apply: timeouts on every call, validate inputs and outputs, and treat third-party servers as untrusted.

The transaction belongs in the application service, around the use case, not in the domain and not in the controller.

BorrowBookService.borrow() is one unit of work: load the book, call book.borrow(...), save it. The service (or a decorator or annotation on it) opens and commits the transaction. The domain stays free of database code, and the controller stays thin. Keep external calls such as sending email out of the transaction: record an event in an outbox table in the same transaction, and send it afterwards.

Often yes for a rich domain, and no for a simple one; the cost is extra code, the gain is a free domain model.

Mapping Book to a BookEntity row (and back) lets the domain use value objects and private fields without ORM annotations or no-arg constructors, and lets the schema change independently. The price is a mapper per aggregate and extra copying. For a small context, annotating the domain class directly is acceptable if you accept the coupling. Choose per bounded context.

code.title: Value object Money vs floating point

followUps:
Store a value object either as several columns in the owner's row, or as one column holding a serialized form.

For Money(1010, "INR") use two columns amount_cents and currency (JPA @Embeddable, EF Core OwnsOne). Small codes like an email can map to one column through a converter. Repeating collections of values can go to a child table with no identity of their own, or a JSON column. The value object has no table identity: its row exists only through its owner, and you replace it rather than update it.

Because binary double cannot store most decimal fractions exactly, so small errors appear and add up.

Example: 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004, and a total that should equal 0.30 fails an equality check. In money that means a ledger that is off by a paisa. Use integer minor units (1010 cents, as in the program), or a decimal type such as BigDecimal, with an explicit rounding mode and a currency stored next to the amount.

A uniqueness rule across all users cannot live inside one small aggregate, so enforce it with a unique index or a reservation step.

The simplest answer is a database unique constraint on email: the insert fails if a duplicate exists, and you translate the error into a domain error. If users live in many databases, use a reservation: first insert email -> userId into a small "claims" table (unique key), then create the user. Do not load every user into one huge aggregate to check it; that kills concurrency.

First ask the business whether they really must change atomically; usually they do not, and a saga or domain event with a compensating step is enough.

Example: transfer 100 between two accounts. Debit account A, publish Debited, then credit B; if credit fails, refund A. If it truly must be atomic (a legal rule), your aggregate boundary is probably wrong and the two belong in one aggregate (for example a Transfer or a single ledger). A last resort is one transaction across two aggregates, accepted knowingly, and only if both sit in the same database.

code.title: Optimistic locking with a version check
code.python:
row = {"value": 100, "version": 1}  # the "database row"


def save(new_value, expected_version):
    """Succeeds only if the version is still the one we read (UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?)."""
    if row["version"] != expected_version:
        return False
    row["value"] = new_value
    row["version"] += 1
    return True


a_val, a_ver = row["value"], row["version"]  # user A reads
b_val, b_ver = row["value"], row["version"]  # user B reads the same version
print("A saves: " + str(save(a_val + 10, a_ver)).lower())
print("B saves: " + str(save(b_val + 20, b_ver)).lower())
# B retries: reload, re-run the command on fresh state, save again
b_val, b_ver = row["value"], row["version"]
print("B retry saves: " + str(save(b_val + 20, b_ver)).lower())
print("final value=%d version=%d" % (row["value"], row["version"]))

followUps:
Tell the user their copy is out of date, show what changed, and let them choose to merge, overwrite or cancel.

The form carries the version it was loaded with (say 7). On save, the server finds version 9 and replies HTTP 409 Conflict with the current data. The UI shows a diff ("Ravi changed the price from 100 to 120") and offers "reload my edit on top". Never silently overwrite: with fields that do not clash, you can merge automatically; for the same field, ask a person.

A lost update is two writers overwriting the same item; write skew is two writers each reading overlapping data and writing different items, breaking a rule neither saw broken.

Lost update: both read stock 10, both write 9, final 9 instead of 8. A version check catches it. Write skew: two doctors both see 2 on call, each goes off call, leaving 0. Their writes touch different rows, so row versions do not clash. Fix with serializable isolation, a lock on the shared row, or by making the rule part of one aggregate.

code.title: Transactional outbox with at-least-once relay and dedupe
code.python:
orders = []      # "orders table"
outbox = []      # outbox table: event ids
sent = set()     # outbox rows marked as sent
broker = []      # the message broker


def place_order(oid):
    # One "transaction": the order row and its event row are written together
    orders.append(oid)
    outbox.append(oid)


def relay(crash_before_marking_last):
    for oid in outbox:
        if oid in sent:
            continue
        broker.append(oid)  # publish
        if crash_before_marking_last and oid == outbox[-1]:
            return  # crash before marking
        sent.add(oid)  # mark sent


place_order(1)
place_order(2)
relay(True)   # crashes after publishing event 2, before marking it
relay(False)  # restart: event 2 is published again (at-least-once)
print("broker: [" + ", ".join(map(str, broker)) + "]")
processed = set()  # consumer dedupe table
for oid in broker:
    if oid not in processed:
        processed.add(oid)
        print("handled event", oid)
    else:
        print("skipped duplicate event", oid)
print("orders=%d outbox=%d" % (len(orders), len(outbox)))

followUps:
A domain event is internal and detailed, while an integration event is a public message to other systems, kept deliberately small and stable.

OrderPlaced inside your service may carry full line items and internal ids, and only your own code reads it. The integration version OrderPlacedV1 sent to other teams carries just the fields they need, in an agreed schema with a version. You map from the first to the second, so renaming an internal field does not break your consumers.

Because the commit and the broker publish cannot be made atomic, and either order loses data when something crashes.

Publish first, then the commit fails: consumers hear about an order that never existed (phantom event). Commit first, then the process dies before publishing: the order exists but nobody is told (lost event). A slow broker call inside the transaction also holds database locks. The outbox writes both rows in one local transaction, so only one system is involved.

code.title: Event sourcing: append, replay, reject
code.python:
store = []  # append-only stream of (type, amount)


def apply(balance, event):  # pure state change, never validates
    kind, amount = event
    return balance + amount if kind == "Deposited" else balance - amount


def load():  # state = fold(events)
    balance = 0
    for e in store:
        balance = apply(balance, e)
    return balance


def handle(cmd, amount):
    version, balance = len(store), load()
    if cmd == "withdraw" and amount > balance:  # decide: validate, may reject
        print("withdraw %d -> rejected: insufficient funds" % amount)
        return
    if len(store) != version:  # expectedVersion check
        raise RuntimeError("concurrent append")
    store.append(("Deposited" if cmd == "deposit" else "Withdrew", amount))
    print("%s %d -> appended" % (cmd, amount))


handle("deposit", 100)
handle("withdraw", 30)
handle("withdraw", 100)
print("events: " + ", ".join("%s %d" % e for e in store))
print("replay: balance=%d version=%d" % (load(), len(store)))

followUps:
You do not edit or delete it; you append a new event that corrects it (a compensating event).

Example: Deposited 1000 was a typo for 100. Append DepositCorrected(was=1000, now=100), or Withdrew 900 with a reason. Replay then produces the right balance, and the audit trail keeps the mistake. Only if the event is plainly invalid (for example it leaks private data) do you do a controlled rewrite of the stream, after a backup, and rebuild projections.

One append-only table with a unique key on stream id plus version gives you both ordering and the optimistic concurrency check.

CREATE TABLE events (
  stream_id TEXT, version INT, type TEXT,
  data JSONB, at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
  global_seq BIGSERIAL,
  PRIMARY KEY (stream_id, version));

Append inserts version = expected+1; a clash raises a unique violation, which you report as a conflict. global_seq lets projections read everything in order.

Migrate it by writing a first event that captures today's state, then switching new changes to events.

Steps: pick one aggregate; for each existing row, append a Migrated (or snapshot-style) event holding its current fields; change the write path to load by replaying and save by appending; keep the old table as a read model fed by projections until you trust it. Do it behind a feature flag, one aggregate type at a time. History before the migration is not recoverable, so say so upfront.

A bounded context is a part of the system inside which every term has one exact meaning, and it is where you choose your architecture style.

"Product" means a catalogue entry for the Catalogue context, but a stock count for Inventory and a price for Billing. Each context owns its model and database, and talks to others through events or APIs. That is why you can event-source Billing, keep Catalogue as plain CRUD, and neither choice leaks into the other.

code.title: Upcasting stored events to the latest version

followUps:
With Avro you rename safely by giving the new field an alias for the old name, so readers can match old data to the new schema.

Writer schema (stored data) has fullName; the reader schema declares name with "aliases": ["fullName"]. Avro resolves the writer's field to the reader's by alias. Adding a field needs a default so old data still reads; removing one is safe if the reader ignores it. Always check compatibility (backward, forward or full) in the schema registry before deploying.

It protects you from a new event version arriving before any code can understand it.

If writers go first, they publish v3 events while half of your consumers only know v2; those consumers crash or skip data. If every reader is upgraded first, they can already handle both v2 and v3, so when the writer starts sending v3 nothing breaks. The same idea as expand-then-contract in database migrations.

Review it against the invariants and the business language, not against whether it compiles.

Checklist: does each rule (for example "total at most 50,000") live in one entity method? Are there setters that bypass it? Are aggregates small, referencing others by id? Are names the ones the domain experts use (OrderPlaced, not OrderUpdatedEvent)? Run property tests and have the model explain a rejected command. AI tends to invent plausible but wrong rules, so check every rule against a person who owns the domain.

Record every agent action as an event in an append-only log, with who, what, why and the result.

Each tool call becomes a command to an aggregate, producing events such as RefundRequested(runId=17, by=agent, reason=...). Because events are never edited, you can replay a run, see exactly what the agent saw and did, and prove nothing was changed afterwards. Store the prompt hash and model version in the event metadata so a bad decision can be traced.
